title: Genevieve (3 January)
hookLine: a young woman who calmed Paris during the siege of Attila

cards: Rumors arrive before armies do. In the story, word reaches Paris that Attila and his Huns are coming, burning cities on the way.
People start loading carts: valuables wrapped in blankets, children on top, the city gates jammed. Neighbors shout advice across the street. Leaving seems like the only sane thing to do.
And one young woman stands in the middle of the panic and says: stay. Don't run. Pray.

teach.h: A CONSECRATED WOMAN IN THE CITY.
teach.b: Genevieve lived in Paris in the days when Roman Gaul was coming apart. An early account of her life tells her story, and the Church remembers her in early January.
She was a consecrated virgin: not a nun in a convent, but a woman who had given her life to God and lived it out in the city, praying, fasting and caring for people.

teach.h: STAY AND PRAY, WHEN EVERYONE RUNS.
teach.b: When the news of Attila came, the account says, she gathered the women of Paris to pray, and she begged the men not to carry their goods away.
The cities they fled to, she warned, would not be safe; Paris would be protected. That did not go down well.
Some citizens called her a false prophet and, the account says, talked about stoning her or throwing her in the river.
Then a churchman arrived from Auxerre, where the bishop Germanus had once praised her, and he spoke up for her, and the crowd backed off.
And Attila's army turned away. It never reached Paris.

teach.h: UNLESS THE LORD KEEP THE CITY.
teach.b: Catholics honor Genevieve as the patron of Paris, and her story sits easily next to a line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it."
What she did is ordinary and very hard. She didn't fight. She didn't flee.
In a crowd that was spinning, she stayed still, prayed, and asked others to do the same. Calm can be contagious. So can panic.
She chose which one to pass on.

how: Catholics keep Saint Genevieve's memory in early January, especially in Paris, where she is honored as the city's patron and people pray for the city in her name.

o: a queen who defended Paris against the Huns
a nun who founded the first convent in Paris
a young woman who urged Paris to stay and pray

p: the bishop who had once praised her

games.q: you're Genevieve. Attila's army is coming and the city is packing to flee. what do you do?
o: gather people to pray and urge them to stay.
go out alone to meet Attila.
games.why: she gathered the women to pray and begged the men not to leave. the crowd turned on her, a churchman from Auxerre defended her, and the army never reached Paris.

practice: Bring your own town to mind, not the whole map, just one street, one hospital, one bus stop, and whatever it's facing now: a storm, a shortage, a fear, a loss. Breathe slowly, the way Genevieve stood still.
If you pray, ask God to keep your city, or ask Saint Genevieve to pray for it; if you don't, hold your city in mind calmly, without fixing anything.

wordCard.voice: Genevieve. A young woman of Paris who, in the story, urged the city to stay and pray when Attila's army came. Patron of Paris, remembered in early January.

orig.note: French: Genevieve, as Parisians say the name of their patron saint.

carryVoice: Your line: she calmed the city. Stillness, passed on. Day nine hundred fifty-three, done.
